Chapter 7: The Tension Between Human and Divine Love
Have you ever felt like your best efforts to love just... aren’t enough? Maybe you try, over and over, but old wounds or stubborn habits trip you up.
It’s a pretty common struggle—wanting to love well, but realizing your own limits. That’s when people often start reaching for something bigger, something beyond themselves.
That’s where this idea of divine love comes in.
Imagine this: there’s a man sitting alone in a quiet church. His hands are folded in his lap, his mind replaying moments he wishes he could take back—people he’s hurt, relationships he’s lost. He aches to make things right, but honestly, he has no idea where to start.
And then, in the hush of that place, he senses something. Not a booming voice, not a blinding vision, just a gentle assurance that he’s not alone. He’s seen—not judged, but truly understood. For a brief moment, forgiveness seems possible. Maybe even a fresh start.
See, divine love isn’t something we can just whip up on our own. It’s a gift—something that comes from outside ourselves. It’s the kind of love that doesn’t dry up, even when everything else does.
It’s what makes forgiveness real and possible. Most of the time, people only catch fleeting glimpses—a moment of unexpected grace, or a deep peace right in the middle of chaos. But you know what? Sometimes, those quick glimpses are enough to keep us going. They spark hope. They help us try again.
But here’s the catch—there’s tension wrapped up in all of this. Most of us want to be self-sufficient. We want to prove we’re worthy, to do it all ourselves. Accepting divine love means saying, “I actually can’t do this alone. I need help.” And that’s not easy.
It’s humbling, accepting a gift you know you could never repay. But at the same time, it’s freeing. You’re reminded you don’t have to be perfect. You really can start over, no matter how many times you’ve messed up.
Here’s something important to remember: divine love doesn’t mean you stop trying to love well. It doesn’t let you off the hook for human effort. Instead, it gives you the strength to keep going—to keep forgiving, to keep reaching out, even when it’s hard.
It’s like the bedrock beneath all other loves—a foundation that never fails, even when everything else falls apart.
